<x_0.0><y_0.0>On cutting fome part of the faffafras tree, or its
fhoots, and holding it to the nofe, it has a frong but
pleafant fmell. Some people peel the root, and boil
the peel with the beer which they are brewing, because
they believe it wholefome. For the fame reafon, the
peel is put into brandy either whill it is distilling or
after it is made. Profeffor Kalm informs us, that a de-
coction of the root of faffafras in water, drank every
morning, is ufed with fuccefs in the dropfy.— When
part of a wood is defined for cultivation, the faffafras
trees are commonly left upon it, because they have a
very thick foliage, and afford a cool shade to the cattle
during the great heats. Some people get their bei-
poffs made of faffafras wood, in order to expel the
bugs; for its frong feent, it is said, prevents thofe
vermin from fettling in them. For two or three years
together this has the defined effect, or about as long-
as the wood keeps its frong aromatic fmell ; but after
that time it has been obferved to lofe its effect. In
Penfylvania fome people put chips of faffafras into
their chefts, where they keep all forts of woollen fluffs,
in order to expel the moths (or larvae or caterpillars of
mothers or tinies) which commonly fettle in them in
fummer. The root keeps its fmell for a long while :
Profeffor Kalm fav one which had lain five or fix years
in the drawer of a table, and fill preferred the strength
of its feent. The people alfo gather its flowers, and
ufe it as tea.<x_0.8213><y_0.4016><class_Text>

<x_0.0166><y_0.4>The _perfea_, or _alligator pear_tree, is cultivated univerfallly
in the Well Indies by all ranks of people. The fruit is
pear-shaped, and from one to two pounds in weight.
On removing a green skin or covering, we come to a
yellow butyraceous fubtlance ; and in the heart find a
large round feed or flone, which is unequal in the fur-
face, and exceedingly hard and woody. This fruit is
ripe in Augull and September, and confitutes one of
the moft agreeable articles of diet for fix or eight
weeks to the negroes. Thefe pears, with a little fall
and a plantain or two, afford a hearty meal. They are
alfo ferved up at the tables of white people as choice
fruit. When the pear is ripe, the yellow or eatable
fubtlance is firmer than butter, and taftes fomewhat
like butter or marrow: hence it is called by fome the
vegetable marrow. But however excellent this fruit is
when ripe, it is very dangerous when pulled and eaten
before maturity. Dr Wright fays, he has repeatedly
known it to produce fever and dyfentery, which were
removed with difficulty.—The leaves of this tree and
thofe of the bead-vine or wild liquorice are made into
pectoral decotions by the common people.—The large
flone is ufed for marking linen. The clothis tied or
held over the flone, and the letters are pricked out by
a needle through the cloth and into the feed. The
flain is a reddish brown, which never wafhes out.—
The buds of the alligator tree are laid to be ufed
with fuccefs in ptifans against the venereal difeafe. An
infusion of them in water, drank in the morning fat-
ing, is strongly recommended for diflodging coagula-
ted blood in the stomach produced by a fall or a fe-
vere froke on that important entrail. " The wild
boars in the East Indies (fays Labat) eat greedily of
the mammeed and avocado pears, which give their flefh
a lufcious and moft agreeable favour."<x_0.8438><y_0.9031><class_Text>
